positions.assign: how it is filled: {words} — information for the leaders
positions.term: term in words, e.g. "3 years, +2 possible"
positions.need: how many are needed in each unit with this position (staffing: “2 missing”)
positions.per: { "count": 4, "of": "uczestnik" } — one person per this many of another position (or per this many places from "intake.limit")
positions.note: note, e.g. "elected in June; at first the pilot couple appoints for a year"

fields.label: label, e.g. "Voice"
fields.options: for "choice": a list of values, e.g. ["sopran", "alt", "tenor", "bas"]
fields.leadersOnly: true — only the leaders see it (health, diet, contact to parents)

units.key: short name (up to 40 characters), e.g. "krag-3"; omitted — from the name
units.name: name, e.g. "Circle 3"
units.kind: kind of area: {kinds}; omitted — from the blueprint or "group"
units.from: key of a blueprint from "blueprints" — the unit takes positions, settings and parts from it; changing the blueprint changes all units made from it, except what a unit set itself
units.positions: position keys of this unit (in addition to those from the blueprint)
units.settings: settings of the five steps (below: Settings); what is missing is inherited
units.council: { "key", "name", "own": [positions of this unit], "below": [positions of the units directly below] } — a council (e.g. a district circle); an area under the unit whose membership follows the staffing
units.people: { "{slot}": ["First Last", "@person-key", …] } — people as a group, e.g. all pupils of 2b; in more detail — in "persons"
units.address: address of the unit's pages, e.g. "dk/rejon-13"; omitted — address of the unit above + "/" + key (at the top: from the community name)
units.area: id of an EXISTING area that becomes this unit and is moved to this place (e.g. two districts under a new diocese) — only deliberately
units.remove: true — dissolved: the community stops managing it (removes the access it gave); the area and its content stay
units.extra: additional parts of the area document — "appointments", "pages", "subforms", "card", "category", "listings", "chats", "publish" — exactly as in the “area” format
units.pagesBy: { "inside": POSITION, "public": POSITION } — who LEADS the unit's addresses (edits the page, opens subpages, can make them public). "inside": the members' page ("dla-nas"; without a public page the unit's address itself); "public": the public page on the unit's address (and "po"). A position of this unit ("para-animatorska") or, with "^", of the unit above ("^para-rejonowa"; "^^" two up). Omitted: whoever imports keeps the address. Inherited only from the blueprint. Leading an address = being able to publish under it: give "public" (or a unit without a public page) only to who may publish

persons.key: short name (omitted — from the full name), e.g. "anna-kowalska"
persons.name: full name — sealed in the units' areas; the service does not see it
persons.places: [{ "unit": "krag-3", "position": "czlonek" }, { "unit": "rejon-13", "position": "para-rejonowa" }] — all places of the person; membership and position are separate
persons.pair: key of the other person of the couple
persons.remove: true — the person leaves: their link stops working

desc.blueprints: Entry in "blueprints": { "key", "name", "kind", "positions", "settings", "council", "extra" } — like a unit, without "units". A unit with "from": "{slot}" takes everything from it that it does not set itself. A blueprint can also be made in the app from an existing unit (“Save as a blueprint”).
desc.usage:
- “Communities” (#/workspace/wspolnoty) shows the tree (a map to drag or a list on the phone), the settings of each unit in five steps with “inherited from …” / “set here” and “Restore inherited”, people with links, staffing (where someone is missing), JSON and the history of changes with “Restore this version”.
- Every unit's area shows “Managed by the community …” with a link; changes made there by hand may be overwritten by the next import.
- A person with a link sees only their own units: chats (with "tools.chat"), a calendar with the dates above (with "visibility.subunitsSee" above), the unit's page (“for us”), “Write to the leaders” ("tools.askLeaders").
- A council has its own chat; it includes the roles of the positions from "own" and "below" — when the staffing changes, the council changes.
- Public sign-up ("intake.mode": "signup") is on the unit's page; those who sign up get the role of the participant position (the first with the right "participant" or "member").
- The field "leadersOnly" and "intake.health" — data for the leaders only (questions in the leaders' sub-form or in the form's requirements).
- What the import does not do by itself (the setting is saved and shown in the unit with the way to the tool): lessons and materials (Scriptorium / Library, in a class — the Class tab), learning with Cogita (review modules on the unit's page), polls downwards, attendance and own tables (a form with leaders' extensions), the place limit and the waiting list (information in the form; counting places is not built).

entries.usage:
- People from the import stand on the form's list like others: in the “Entries” tab (marked “no link”), in the “Table”, on the “Attendance list” of tasks with dates and in the page modules “List of people” and “Person panel”.
- Records from "records" stand in the extension's sheet, period by period — with history, summary, “Print list” and “Download CSV”.
- Only the form's coordinators open the answers; whoever runs the page but does not read the answer area sees only that there are records. The CSV from the “Table” and the export of this JSON contain decrypted answers — nothing protects such a file any more.
- An added person does not see their entry, does not fill in sub-forms, gets neither participant roles ("memberRoles") nor a one-to-one conversation; the office ticks their steps, tasks and attendance, and a person area from "virtualAreas" (if the form has one) serves only the office.
- The import does not ring: the bell and notifications count only entries sent by the people themselves. It also works on a closed form.
entries.descTitle: List of people of the form “{name}” as JSON ("{format}", version 1)
entries.descIntro:
What the import does here: it ADDS people to this form's list and CHANGES the details of people already on it; in extensions filled in by the coordinator it adds and changes records (separately for each period). It deletes nothing. Everything is sealed in this browser before it reaches the service.
- A person with an "id" from the export is changed. A person without an "id" is created new — unless there is exactly one person with the same first name and surname on the list: then it is them.
- Only the answers that are in the document are changed; the rest stays.
- The import does not change the answers of a person who signed up themselves and has their own link.
- An added person has no link of their own — the coordinator looks after them.

lab2d.bakeCpuOnly: The processor bakes this scene: the graphics card does not compute carved ice, salt grains or more than eight moving bodies yet.
lab2d.bakeNearCap: That is almost all the space for recordings in this browser (600 MB) — older recordings will be removed.
lab2d.bakeOverCap: That is more than the space for recordings in this browser (600 MB) — shorten the recording or choose fewer resume points or a coarser grid.
lab2d.bakeNoWebgpu: This browser has no WebGPU — the processor bakes.
lab2d.bakeGpuFailed: The graphics card did not start — the processor bakes.
lab2d.bakeGpuLost: The graphics card stopped responding — what is already baked is saved.
lab2d.bakeTitleAccel: Bake a recording — switches to the normal view (the graphics card can bake there too).
lab2d.clipPlayAccel: Play the recording — switches to the normal view.
lab2d.clipFromCpu: This recording was baked by the processor.
lab2d.clipFromGpu: This recording was baked by the graphics card.
lab2d.clipToCpu: Show the processor’s recording (at the same moment).
lab2d.clipToGpu: Show the graphics card’s recording (at the same moment).
lab2d.clipLiveGpuTitle: Computes on live from the last resume point before this frame (a graphics-card recording cannot be repeated bit for bit) — in the accelerated view where the browser supports it.
lab2d.extBodyBubble: The vapour bubble is already {r} mm — the water is superheated and boils explosively.
lab2d.extLater: You can change this in the settings.
lab2d.saved: Scene saved as a JSON file.
lab2d.refused: Refused: the liquid would have no free surface (such a region has no pressure in this model).
lab2d.slow: The computer cannot keep up: the simulation runs at {x}× real time.
lab2d.slowLowest: This is already the coarsest grid. Time runs slower, the results stay the same.
lab2d.buoyancyRatio: Buoyancy is {x} times the weight of the bubble.
lab2d.bubbleHint: Click a bubble with “Inspect” to see its forces.
lab2d.title: 2D lab
lab2d.accelTitle: Open the accelerated view: the whole model runs on the graphics card (WebGPU), on a 1 mm grid.
lab2d.accelNoOther: The accelerated view does not know carved ice (several rectangles), salt grains, more than eight moving bodies or more than 128 body contacts at once yet — this scene runs in the normal view.
lab2d.accelFailed: The accelerated view did not start (this browser or graphics card has no WebGPU) — back to the normal view.
lab2d.objPinned: Pinned — stays put, does not fall
lab2d.objAtStart: Size, material and temperature change during setup — after “Restart”.
lab2d.arrowsNote: Arrows: gas up to {g} cm/s (dark), water up to {w} cm/s (white) — each on its own scale.
lab2d.oxygenNote: Applies to the air that flows in through open sides — the gas in the box keeps its composition.
lab2d.fateBurst: This bubble reached the surface and burst — its vapour escaped into the air. Below is its last state.
lab2d.fateCollapsed: This bubble vanished: its vapour condensed in the cooler water. Below is its last state.
lab2d.fateMerged: This bubble merged with another one — the merged bubble is shown now.
lab2d.whyRise: Why does the bubble rise? The water pushes harder from below than from above (buoyancy) — and vapour weighs almost nothing.
lab2d.aboutLead: Every model simplifies reality — that is a lesson too. Here is what this model leaves out or approximates.
lab2d.bakeTitle: Bake a recording: the scene is computed once, as fast as the computer allows, and stored in this browser — then it plays back smoothly without computing.
lab2d.bakeStopTitle: Stop baking — what is already computed stays as a shorter recording
lab2d.bakeFailed: The recording could not be baked
lab2d.bakeShort: The recording was too short to keep.
lab2d.seeking: Preparing the state of this moment… {p} %
lab2d.clipLiveTitle: Computes on live from exactly this frame — from the nearest stored state, bit for bit as when baking.
lab2d.clipEngine: The recording was made by another version of the engine — bake it again to continue live.
lab2d.clipTools: Tools work live — click “Live from here”.
lab2d.clipAccel: Baking and recordings work in the normal view.

ai.aiFormat:
Scene “2D lab” — JSON. The engine computes everything from the laws of physics and the materials database; the scene only says what stands where at the start (the starting setup, not the course of events).
Units: metres (origin in the lower left corner of the inside of the box, y upwards), temperatures in °C, pressure in kPa, power in W (per layer thickness).

{ "format": "recreatio/lab2d", "version": 1, "seed": number (repeatable randomness),
  "box": { "w": width (0.2), "h": height (0.15), "depth": thickness of the 2D layer (0.01) },
  "ambient": { "p": kPa (101.325), "T": °C, "rh": humidity 0–1, "g": m/s² (from 2.45 to 19.6), "air": { "N2": 0.7676, "O2": 0.2324 } },
  "sides": { "left" | "right" | "bottom" | "top": "wall" or "open" (an open side is the room) },
  "quality": "high" (2 mm cells, usual) | "very-high" (1 mm) | "medium" (3 mm),
  "extremes": "ask" (default: the lab asks when boiling turns violent) | "compute" (compute exactly — superheated water may boil explosively) | "normalize" (soften — calm boiling), optional,
  "ops": [ build steps in order ] }

Objects — "body" (block, ice cube, stone), "beaker", "hotplate" — have a name "id" (e.g. "cube", "beaker"; without one they get "body-1", "beaker-1" …) and their own settings: "pinned" (stays put, does not fall), "T", "angle", material, size, heating. A setting is changed in the object itself, not in a separate step.

Steps ("op"):
  { "op": "fill", "region": region, "composition": { "H2O": 1 }, "phase": "liquid", "T": °C } — liquid in the region: "H2O" (water) or "oil-rapeseed" (rapeseed oil; does not evaporate, lighter than water, thicker in motion); several liquids at once (mass fractions) spread evenly and separate under gravity; "NaCl" (table salt) dissolves in water: { "H2O": 0.9, "NaCl": 0.1 } is 10 % brine (saturated is about 26 %; the excess crystallises as a crust on the bottom, brine boils above 100 °C); "phase": "gas" with { "N2": 0.7676, "O2": 0.2324 } — air
  { "op": "erase", "region": region } — removes water, bubbles, crystals and solids; room air comes back
  { "op": "grains", "region": region, "material": "NaCl", "d": crystal diameter in m (0.0005 — table salt; from 0.00005 to 0.005), "T": °C } — a handful of salt crystals (loosely poured): falls, sinks in water the slower the finer the crystals (water drag), forms a heap with slopes of about 34°, dissolves where the water is not saturated (cooling it slightly; without stirring the salty water stays at the bottom), in saturated brine the crystals grow; in superheated water the air in the cracks of the crystals triggers sudden boiling
  { "op": "move", "id": object name, "dx": m, "dy": m } — moves an object together with what lies inside its outline (water and bubbles in a beaker, an ice cube in it); this is how a drag with the “Select” tool is recorded. Or { "op": "move", "region": region, "dx", "dy" } — everything solid in the region (a painted structure, by whole cells)
  { "op": "remove", "id": object name } — takes an object away
  { "op": "solid", "region": region, "material": "glass" | "steel" | "ceramic" | "wood" | "ice" | "stone", "T": °C } — a fixed structure made of grid cells (ceramic = boiling chips; ice as a structure does not melt — melting ice is a "body")
  { "op": "body", "id": name, "region": region, "material": "wood" | "ice" | "stone" | "glass" | "steel" | "ceramic", "T": °C, "pinned": true (optional: pinned, stays put), "angle": degrees (optional, rotation about the centre) } — an object: an exact rectangle (a circle becomes a square of the same area, a polygon the rectangle enclosing it, a line with width a rotated rectangle); a free one falls, floats, sinks and tips over (wood 510 kg/m³ floats, ice 917 kg/m³ floats almost fully submerged, stone sinks); ice melts when it is warm and freezes on in water colder than its freezing point — it stays a rectangle, a whole face recedes or grows; in brine it melts below 0 °C (a freezing mixture)
  { "op": "beaker", "id": name, "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w": width, "h": height, "wall": wall thickness, "material": "glass", "T": °C, "lid": true (optional, tight lid), "pinned": false (optional: a free beaker — it may tip over), "angle": degrees (optional, rotation about the centre of the bottom) } — a beaker (cross-section); without "pinned": false it stands pinned
  { "op": "hotplate", "id": name, "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w", "h", "material": "steel", "mode": "power" | "thermostat", "power": W, "target": °C, "on": true, "T": °C, "pinned": false (optional) } — a hot plate (pinned unless "pinned": false)
Region: { "rect": [x0, y0, x1, y1] } | { "circle": [x, y, r] } | { "poly": [[x, y], …] } | { "line": [x0, y0, x1, y1], "width": thickness }
A liquid must have a free surface (gas above it) — a completely flooded closed region is rejected.
ai.aiPrompt:
Prepare a JSON starting setup for the “2D lab” module in REcreatio (a school sandbox: heat, boiling, evaporation, fog, water, oil and brine, salt crystals that sink and dissolve, bodies that fall, float and sink, ice that melts and freezes on).
Topic: [describe what should stand in the box, e.g. “a beaker of hot water on a hot plate, boiling chips on the bottom”].
Rules: real sizes (beaker 7 cm wide, plate 12 cm), things do not overlap, apparatus stands on the bottom (y = 0) or on another thing, water inside the beaker above its bottom; a free object may hang above the water — it will fall (unless it has "pinned": true). Give objects short "id" names. Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

flatWorld.title: Flat world
flatWorld.primary: The box is flat like the pane of a 1 cm thick aquarium. Nothing flows forwards or backwards.
flatWorld.secondary: A 2D layer of thickness D = 1 cm; the front and back walls give off no heat. Bubbles are spheres while they are narrower than the layer, then discs.

grid.title: Grid of 1–3 mm
grid.primary: Temperature and pressure are computed in 2 mm cells. Things smaller than a cell are approximated.
grid.secondary: Fields on 1–3 mm cells; the thin boundary layer at the walls is not resolved — it is replaced by the contact temperature T_f = (k_s T_s + k_l T_l)/(k_s + k_l).

waterAirApart.title: Water and air apart
waterAirApart.primary: Water and air are computed separately: to the water the air is only a pressure, to the air the water is a moving wall.
waterAirApart.secondary: Two separate pressure projections (density ratio ~830 : 1); air trapped in water is not modelled (MultiFLIP is the way forward).

noSound.title: No sound
noSound.primary: There are no sound waves and no explosions in this model.
noSound.secondary: Low Mach number gas: density from temperature and composition at the region pressure p0.

incompressible.title: Water does not compress
incompressible.primary: Water cannot be compressed, but warm water is lighter and rises.
incompressible.secondary: Projection with constant density and gravity g·ρ(T)/ρ_ref — buoyancy from the true density, with its maximum at 4 °C.

tensionInBubbles.title: Surface tension only in bubbles
tensionInBubbles.primary: Drops and the meniscus are not shaped by surface tension. That is why gravity is at least 1/4 of Earth’s.
tensionInBubbles.secondary: The capillary length of water (~2.7 mm) is about one cell; surface tension acts in the bubble models (pressure inside, nucleation, detachment).

noRadiation.title: No radiation
noRadiation.primary: Heat flows by contact and motion, not by glowing.
noRadiation.secondary: No thermal radiation: a very hot plate loses less heat than it really would.

lossesOneNumber.title: Losses as one number
lossesOneNumber.primary: The room behind the box is not computed — the walls lose heat according to one number.
lossesOneNumber.secondary: h_ext = 10 W/(m²·K) on the walls of the box, in series with half a cell.

cavities.title: Pits in the walls
cavities.primary: Bubbles are born in tiny pits in the walls. Boiling chips have many large ones.
cavities.secondary: Up to 8 cavities per wall cell, radii from a power-law distribution (steel after Lemmert and Chawla); activation at T_f − T_sat ≥ ΔT_act.

bubbleFormulas.title: Bubbles from formulas
bubbleFormulas.primary: Growth, detachment and motion of bubbles are computed by formulas tested in laboratories (accurate to about 10–20 %).
bubbleFormulas.secondary: Growth: Plesset–Zwick and Ranz–Marshall; detachment: Fritz; drag: Tomiyama (contaminated water); no lift force and no collisions other than merging.

idealGases.title: Ideal gases
idealGases.primary: Air is nitrogen and oxygen; vapour behaves like an ideal gas.
idealGases.secondary: The enthalpy of vapour depends only on T; the heat of vaporisation away from 100 °C follows Kirchhoff’s law (0.5 % too low at 20 °C).

fogNoFall.title: Fog does not settle
fogNoFall.primary: Fog flows with the air and does not fall like rain.
fogNoFall.secondary: Fog is a mass per cell carried with the gas; dew settles only on the walls.

liquidsOneFlow.title: Several liquids, one flow
liquidsOneFlow.primary: Water and oil flow in a shared velocity field; each liquid has its own density, so oil floats on water.
liquidsOneFlow.secondary: Projection with a constant (mean) density, gravity from the density of each particle — hydrostatics exact in every layer, inertia approximate (good for density ratios of about 0.7–1.5).

viscosity.title: Viscosity only where it matters
viscosity.primary: Oil flows “thickly”, water almost without friction — because in 2 mm cells the friction of water is negligible.
viscosity.secondary: Viscosity computed implicitly in the simplified form ∇·(η∇u), only when the scene holds a liquid other than water; the liquid sticks to the walls, the free surface has no stress.

subcellDrops.title: Drops smaller than a cell
subcellDrops.primary: A droplet of oil in water (or of water in oil) rises or sinks at the speed a real drop of that size would have.
subcellDrops.secondary: A particle surrounded by another liquid drifts at the terminal velocity of a drop of its volume (Schiller–Naumann drag, Hadamard–Rybczynski correction). There is no tension between the liquids — drops are not round, and an emulsion separates faster than a real fine one.

onlyWaterEvaporates.title: Only water evaporates
onlyWaterEvaporates.primary: Oil does not evaporate, smoke or burn. A vapour bubble in oil simply passes through it.
onlyWaterEvaporates.secondary: Oil has no vapour pressure in the model; a vapour bubble in oil neither grows nor condenses; oil data measured at 20–160 °C, extrapolated above.

saltInWater.title: Salt in water
saltInWater.primary: Salt dissolved in water raises the boiling point and lowers the freezing point. All of it follows from one quantity: the water activity.
saltInWater.secondary: Water activity from the Pitzer equations (PHREEQC parameters, below 0 °C Spencer–Møller–Weare): vapour pressure over brine a_w·p_sat, boiling at a_w·p_sat(T_b) = p, freezing from the equilibrium with ice. Density and specific heat of brine after Laliberté. Salts other than NaCl: later stages.

saltMixing.title: Salt mixes when the water flows
saltMixing.primary: Salty and fresh water brought together in one cell by the flow even out within seconds while the water flows, and within minutes while it stands still. Between cells salt spreads by itself very slowly — millimetres per hour; further on, the moving water carries it.
saltMixing.secondary: Ion diffusion: D = 1.61·10⁻⁹ m²/s at 25 °C (Nernst–Hartley mean), at other temperatures after Stokes–Einstein. In still water every particle approaches the mean salt content of its cell with the time τ = Δx²/(π² D) (4.8 min at 2 mm and 20 °C). Flowing water stretches what is in the cell into ever thinner bands (stretching λ) — salt diffuses quickly across a thin band: mixing time t = W(2λτ)/(2λ) (W — Lambert function; Ranz 1979, Villermaux 2019), 2.4 s at λ = 1/s. Between cells Fick’s law. D does not depend on concentration here (in reality it drops by about 8 % at 1 mol/kg).

crystalsOnBottom.title: Crystals straight onto the bottom
crystalsOnBottom.primary: When water goes away and the solution is saturated, the excess salt settles at once as a white crust on the nearest wall below — or grows on a salt crystal lying nearby. The crust does not dissolve again.
crystalsOnBottom.secondary: The excess above solubility (Pitzer, Peiper and Busey 1984) passes at once onto a crystal in the same or a neighbouring cell, and without one into a crust on the nearest solid cell (no supersaturation; no new crystals form in the liquid); the heat of crystallisation stays in the liquid. The crust does not dissolve back — only crystals dissolve.

roundGrains.title: Salt crystals as round grains
roundGrains.primary: Poured salt is crystals, but in the model one grain stands for many real ones, is round and does not roll. Friction is chosen so that a heap of salt has slopes of about 34° — like real fine salt.
roundGrains.secondary: Grain particles (each standing for N crystals of diameter d, four per cell at a packing of 0.58) are discs without rotation; contact and friction (static μ = 0.245, kinetic 0.2) as position constraints (PBD, Macklin et al. 2014), lower grains count as heavier — the heap stands at once. The angle of repose of fine salt, 34 ± 3°, is a cited value (no measurement for 0.3–0.8 mm); a single heap scatters by ±2°. Grains take space from the water but not from the air.

saltSinks.title: Salt sinks and dissolves
saltSinks.primary: Crystals sink in water as fast as real ones of that size and dissolve only where the water is not yet saturated — dissolving cools the water slightly. In superheated water a bubble is born on every dry crystal.
saltSinks.secondary: Settling velocity after Ferguson and Church (2004), implicit drag, force passed to the water; density and temperature from the water particles in the grain’s cell, viscosity of pure water (saturated brine has almost twice as much). Dissolution ṁ = A k ρ ln(1 + B), k = Sh D/d, Sh = 1 + (1 + Re·Sc)^⅓ f(Re) (Clift et al.); salt enters the water with the enthalpy of the crystal (heat of solution +4.6 kJ/mol at 20 °C, negative at 100 °C). The cracks of dry crystals hold air: they act like a wall cavity with a radius of 10 µm (about 3.3 K of superheat) and give a bubble at most every 25 ms — for 2 s in water, then they are flooded (model assumptions).

airDroplets.title: Droplets in the air
airDroplets.primary: A splash or a leftover of water smaller than a cell boils when it is hotter than the boiling point, but below it does not evaporate.
airDroplets.secondary: Particles in a cell that is not liquid: above T_boil they evaporate into their cell (a drop that evaporated completely leaves its salt as a crust), two cells away from the liquid they fly ballistically; there is no evaporation below T_boil — a drop on a cold wall does not dry.

iceWholeWalls.title: Ice melts by whole faces
iceWholeWalls.primary: An ice cube melts when it is warm and freezes onto itself in cold water — but it stays a rectangle: a whole face recedes or grows at once, and the corners stay sharp. Water away from ice does not freeze, even when very cold.
iceWholeWalls.secondary: Heat inside the ice above the melting point passes at once to the face through which heat flows in (water, air, hot plate) and moves it evenly; water colder than T_f in front of the face freezes on. The front lies in cells: first-order accuracy in Δx — the Neumann solution within 6–7 % at 2 mm. Ice forms only on ice (no nucleation and no frost); vapour pressure below 0 °C as at 0 °C. Water from under a cube lying on the plate flows out at its two edges (there is no water film under the cube), and the last quarter of an ice cell melts in one step.

heatInCell.title: Heat evens out within a cell
heatInCell.primary: A hot and a cold water particle in the same cell even out their temperature within seconds — as fast as water conducts.
heatInCell.secondary: The grid conducts heat between cells; within a cell every particle approaches the mean temperature of the cell with the time τ = Δx²/(π² α), α = k/(ρ c_p) (water at 20 °C: 2.8 s at 2 mm, 0.7 s at 1 mm; IEM model) — in flowing water too: faster evening out in the cell would carry the heat of a hot wall into the neighbouring cells, and the water at the boiling chips would be too cold. The energy of the cell stays exactly the same; a drop alone in the air exchanges no heat with others.

roomBehindSide.title: The room behind an open side
roomBehindSide.primary: Behind an open side there is ordinary room air.
roomBehindSide.secondary: Inflow brings ambient air; what flows out is counted as “escaped”.

rigidBodies.title: Bodies as wholes
rigidBodies.primary: A beaker, a plate, a wooden block or an ice cube are rigid wholes: pinned they stay put, unpinned they fall, float, sink and tip over. Wood floats half submerged, ice almost completely. A body floating in a small vessel rocks slightly (by less than a cell).
rigidBodies.secondary: A body is a few exact rectangles (they lie between cells and at an angle; each of their inner cells has its own energy) with position, velocity, mass and moment of inertia; collisions as in Physics 2D (SAT, warm start, Coulomb friction). The grid sees the body as fractions covering the cells and their faces, so buoyancy changes smoothly with position. The force of water and air is the pressure on the true outline; the mass of water moved with the body is measured by an extra solve of the pressure projection. A gap narrower than half a cell is not seen: a cell covered by 99 % (by an unpinned body already by 90 %) counts as full, and a small air pocket (under 2 cm³) closed only by an unpinned body counts as open — its air escapes. A falling square has too little drag (C_D about 1.8 instead of 2.1), because its wake has no time to shed alternately.

frictionlessWalls.title: Walls without friction
frictionlessWalls.primary: Water slides along the walls without friction. At a real wall a thin film of water stands still.
frictionlessWalls.secondary: Free slip at the walls (mirrored nodes in APIC): the boundary layer is much thinner than a cell.

onlyBubbles.title: Only bubbles in water
onlyBubbles.primary: No empty spaces can form inside water — gas in water is only bubbles.
onlyBubbles.secondary: A cell becomes gas only when it was gas or borders gas: there is no cavitation and no air bubbles entrained by splashing. Gas that would still remain in a cell with water (e.g. vapour from a bubble that collapsed where there is no water any more) passes at once to the nearest cell with air.

violentBoiling.title: Violent boiling
violentBoiling.primary: A very hot wall gives bubbles at most as much heat as real boiling lets through. With “Soften” boiling is calmer than in reality: large bubbles escape into the air at once, and water does not fly out of the vessel. “Ask” pauses the simulation when boiling turns violent.
violentBoiling.secondary: Heat to a bubble on the wall limited by the critical heat flux q″ = 0.149 ρ_v^½ h_lv [σ g (ρ_l − ρ_v)]^¼ (Lienhard and Dhir 1973; 1.26 MW/m² at 1 atm); there is no transition or film boiling (Leidenfrost). A bubble larger than a cell is still an object: it pushes water away by its volume fraction and a ring of water around it, and does not deform. “Soften”: 1/10 of the flux, nucleation at the latest at 2 K of superheat, bubbles at most 4 mm (the rest goes to the air), water at most 1.5 m/s — with exact mass and energy.

tinyBubbles.title: Many tiny bubbles
tinyBubbles.primary: At a hot bottom more tiny bubbles are born than in reality; most of them vanish at once.
tinyBubbles.secondary: One wall cell (2 mm) holds the whole superheat at the wall, so a cavity is ready again quickly; in subcooled water thousands of bubbles per second are born and collapse. The energy is right, the number of bubbles is too high.

fogWhiteness.title: How white the fog is
fogWhiteness.primary: Fog is drawn as if you were looking through the whole beaker, not through a thin 1 cm layer.
fogWhiteness.secondary: Opacity from the Beer–Lambert law for droplets with a radius of 1.5 µm along a path of 7 cm. The amount of fog is computed, its whiteness is an assumption.

beakerOnPlate.title: Beaker of water on a hot plate
beakerOnPlate.summary: boiling scene: water (20 °C) in a glass beaker with boiling chips on a steel hot plate
beakerOnPlate.text:
The beaker holds water at room temperature, with a 40 W hot plate under it. Watch how first the plate heats up, then the glass, then the water.
Bubbles appear at the bottom. While the water is cool, they vanish before they reach the surface. The “Water temperature” chart will show a plateau at the boiling point.

boilingChips.title: Boiling with chips
boilingChips.summary: water just below boiling (98 °C) on a hot plate — nucleate boiling shows at once
boilingChips.text:
The water is at 98 °C, the plate is hot. Boiling chips have many pits in which bubbles are born — the water boils calmly, without superheating.
Inspect a bubble with the “Inspect” tool: its buoyancy is hundreds of times its weight.

pressureCooker.title: Pressure cooker — a closed box
pressureCooker.summary: the same beaker, but the box is closed: the pressure rises and the water boils at a higher temperature
pressureCooker.text:
The box is sealed. As the water evaporates, the vapour has no way out — the pressure rises, and so does the boiling point.
Compare the boiling point in the inspector with an open box.

waterUnderOil.title: Water under oil
waterUnderOil.summary: hot water (97 °C) under a layer of oil on a hot plate — vapour bubbles break through the oil
waterUnderOil.text:
Oil is lighter than water and does not mix with it, so it floats on top. Below it the water starts to boil.
Vapour bubbles are born only in the water and pass through the oil — the oil itself does not evaporate (up to its smoke point, about 200 °C).

oilWaterSeparate.title: Oil and water separate
oilWaterSeparate.summary: water and oil mixed half and half — gravity separates them: the oil rises to the top
oilWaterSeparate.text:
The beaker holds a fine mixture of water and oil. Oil is lighter (920 kg/m³), so its droplets rise while the water sinks.
Oil also flows much more “thickly”: at 20 °C its viscosity is almost a hundred times that of water — that is why separating takes time.

brineBoilsLater.title: Brine boils later
brineBoilsLater.summary: two beakers on two plates: water on the left, brine (15 % salt) on the right — the brine boils at a higher temperature
brineBoilsLater.text:
Pure water on the left, brine with 15 % salt on the right; both are at 97 °C and stand on identical plates.
Water starts to boil at 100 °C, brine only at about 103 °C. Inspect both with the “Inspect” tool: the inspector shows the temperature at which the liquid boils at that spot.
Salt does not evaporate: as water escapes as vapour, the brine gets saltier and saltier (the “Salt content” overlay).

brineEvaporation.title: Evaporating brine
brineEvaporation.summary: a thin layer of nearly saturated brine (25 %) on a plate at 250 °C — the water boils off, a white salt crust remains on the bottom
brineEvaporation.text:
The beaker holds a thin layer of brine with 25 % salt — almost as much as water can dissolve. A thermostat keeps the plate at 250 °C.
The water boils and evaporates, the salt stays. Once the solution is saturated, the excess salt crystallises and settles on the bottom as a white crust — until all the water is gone.
In the developer panel the “NaCl” balance shows that no salt is lost: all of it ends up in the crust.

fog.title: Fog over hot water
fog.summary: hot water (90 °C) in a cool, humid room — fog forms above the beaker
fog.text:
The water in the beaker is hot, the room is cool. Water vapour is invisible — white fog forms only where the humid air cools down.
Turn on the “Water vapour” overlay to see the invisible vapour next to the visible fog.

mountain.title: Boiling in the mountains
mountain.summary: the same beaker at a pressure of 70 kPa (about 3000 m above sea level) — water boils at only about 90 °C
mountain.text:
High in the mountains the air pressure is lower: here 70 kPa instead of 101 kPa. Water then boils at a lower temperature — about 90 °C.
Inspect the water with the “Inspect” tool: the inspector shows the boiling point at that spot. Compare with “Boiling with chips”.

convection.title: Convection above a heater
convection.summary: a small heater in cold water — warm water rises, cool water sinks and a vortex forms
convection.text:
A small heater (6 W) lies in cold water, at the bottom on the left. Heated water is lighter and rises above it, cooler water sinks on the other side — a vortex forms.
Turn on the “Temperature” overlay, then “Velocity” (white arrows show how the water flows).

brineUnderWater.title: Brine under fresh water
brineUnderWater.summary: a layer of brine (20 %) under fresh water, the plate heats from below — the layers do not mix
brineUnderWater.text:
Brine with 20 % salt lies at the bottom of the beaker, fresh water above it. The plate heats from below: the brine circulates and warms up, but stays at the bottom — even warm it is heavier than the water above it.
The “Salt content” overlay shows that the boundary stays sharp (salt crosses it only by diffusion, millimetres per hour). The “Temperature” overlay shows that heat crosses the boundary much faster.

whatFloats.title: What floats?
whatFloats.summary: a wooden block, an ice cube and a stone fall into cold water — wood floats, ice almost fully submerged, the stone sinks
whatFloats.text:
Three bodies hang above the water: a pine block, an ice cube and a stone (granite). Let time run — they fall into the water.
Wood (510 kg/m³) sinks halfway, ice (917 kg/m³) almost completely, and the stone (2630 kg/m³) goes to the bottom. A floating body displaces as much water as it weighs itself — inspect them with the “Inspect” tool.
The water is at 2 °C, so the ice melts slowly: it stays a rectangle that gets smaller over time. Click an object with the “Select” tool: tick “Pinned” in the “Object” panel and it stays where it hangs.

iceInWarmWater.title: Ice in warm water
iceInWarmWater.summary: an ice cube (−10 °C) floats in water at 40 °C and melts — it stays a rectangle, and water appears in its place
iceInWarmWater.text:
An ice cube (3 cm, −10 °C) floats in water at 40 °C — almost entirely under water. It melts from all sides at once: it stays a rectangle that gets smaller and smaller, and water appears in its place.
The “Temperature” overlay shows the cold water from the melting ice: it flows downwards, because cold water is heavier than warm water. The energy balance stays closed — the heat of the water goes into melting the ice: 334 J for every gram.

iceWithSalt.title: Ice with salt — a freezing mixture
iceWithSalt.summary: three ice cubes float in strong brine (23 %) — the ice melts below 0 °C and cools the brine far below zero
iceWithSalt.text:
Three ice cubes float in brine with 23 % salt. Salt lowers the melting point of ice: in such brine ice still melts at −20 °C and takes heat from it, so the brine cools far below 0 °C. This is a freezing mixture — ice cream used to be made in one.
Water from the melting ice dilutes the brine, and weaker brine freezes at a higher temperature: the mixture stops at the freezing point of its brine and never goes below the eutectic (−21.2 °C). The “Inspect” tool shows the freezing point of the brine at that spot.

saltIntoWater.title: Salt poured into water
saltIntoWater.summary: a handful of salt (0.5 mm crystals) falls into cold water — it sinks, dissolves slowly, and salty water collects at the bottom
saltIntoWater.text:
A handful of salt hangs above a beaker of water at 20 °C. Let time run: the crystals fall, slow down in the water and settle on the bottom at a few centimetres per second (water drag), forming a heap.
Salt dissolves only where the water is not yet saturated. Dense brine forms at the bottom and stays down — without stirring, dissolving takes a long time. The “Salt content” overlay shows the salty layer, and “Temperature” that dissolving cools it slightly.

saltSuperheated.title: Salt into superheated water
saltSuperheated.summary: water superheated to 104 °C (without chips) and a pinch of salt — the cracks of the crystals hold air, so the water suddenly boils on every grain
saltSuperheated.text:
The water in the beaker is at 104 °C — above the boiling point, but smooth glass has no pits in which a bubble could form, so the water does not boil (it is superheated). A pinch of salt hangs above it.
The crystals have cracks with air in them. When they fall into the superheated water, vapour bubbles are born on each one — the water boils violently until the superheat is used up. The lab will pause and ask how to go on: exactly (water may fly out of the vessel) or more gently. This happens in kitchens with water from a microwave. Salt does not cool the water here: at 100 °C dissolving it gives off a little heat.

tippedBeaker.title: A tipping beaker
tippedBeaker.summary: a beaker of water stands on the edge of a stone step, too far out — it tips over and the water spills
tippedBeaker.text:
A beaker of water (free, not pinned) stands on the edge of a step so that its centre of gravity is already beyond the edge. Let time run — the beaker turns around the edge and falls, and the water spills.
Click the beaker with the “Select” tool: tick “Pinned” in the “Object” panel and the beaker stays put. Drag it closer to the wall of the step and untick “Pinned” — if its centre of gravity is above the step, it stays.

emptyBox.title: Empty box
emptyBox.summary: a box full of air — paint water, draw walls, add objects: ice cubes, blocks, beakers, hot plates
emptyBox.text: The box is full of air. Paint water, draw walls and add objects (an ice cube, a wooden block, a stone, a beaker, a hot plate) — free ones fall, float or sink, ice melts. Click an object with the “Select” tool to change its settings, e.g. “Pinned” — then it does not fall.

labParticles.title: Particle lab
labParticles.slow: This computer cannot keep up: the simulation runs at {x}× real time.
labParticles.slowLowest: This is already the lowest level. Time runs slower, but the results stay the same.
labParticles.m1Note: Stage M1a: mechanics — liquid and gas, walls, surface tension, buoyancy. Heat and boiling come next.
labParticles.airNote: Air far from everything is computed without particles: still, at room temperature (the background of the box). Air particles exist only near liquids and apparatus.
labParticles.fullPowerTitle: Open the lab in a new tab — it computes on every processor core
labParticles.fullPowerSlow: In a new tab the lab computes on every core:
labParticles.hintPaint: Drag across the box to paint with the chosen material.
labParticles.hintErase: Drag to erase — air comes back into the empty space.
labParticles.hintPlace: Click where the chosen apparatus should stand (its bottom at the click).
labParticles.hintWall: Drag from the start to the end of the wall.
labParticles.hintInspect: Click a particle to see its data.
labParticles.noWebgl2: This browser does not support WebGL2 — the lab computes but does not draw.

ai.format:
Particle lab scene (module “Particle lab”) — JSON. The engine computes everything from local rules and the substance database; the scene only says what stands where at the start (it is the starting setup, not the course of events).
Units: metres (origin in the lower left corner of the inside of the box, y upwards), temperatures in °C, pressure in kPa, power in W (per layer thickness).

{ "format": "recreatio/particles", "version": 1, "seed": number (repeatable randomness),
  "box": { "w": width, "h": height, "depth": thickness of the 2D layer (usually 0.01) },
  "ambient": { "p": kPa (101.325), "T": °C, "g": m/s² (0 — weightlessness), "air": { "N2": 0.7676, "O2": 0.2324 } },
  "sides": { "left" | "right" | "bottom" | "top": "wall" or "open" (an open side is the room) },
  "quality": "very-high" | "high" | "medium" (particle size 2 / 2.5 / 3 mm; usually "very-high"),
  "ops": [ build steps in order ] }

Steps ("op"):
  { "op": "fill", "region": region, "composition": { substance: mass fraction }, "phase": "liquid" | "gas", "T": °C } — fills the region with liquid or gas (whatever was there gives way)
  { "op": "erase", "region": region } — removes everything in the region; air comes back
  { "op": "solid", "region": region, "material": material, "T": °C } — a fixed solid (a wall, boiling chips)
  { "op": "beaker", "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w": width, "h": height, "wall": wall thickness, "material": "glass" } — a beaker (cross-section)
  { "op": "hotplate", "x": centre, "y": bottom, "w", "h", "material": "steel", "mode": "power" | "thermostat", "power": W, "target": °C, "on": true } — a hot plate
Region: { "rect": [x0, y0, x1, y1] } | { "circle": [x, y, r] } | { "poly": [[x, y], …] } | { "line": [x0, y0, x1, y1], "width": thickness }
ai.prompt:
Prepare a JSON starting setup for the “Particle lab” module in REcreatio (a 2D school sandbox made of particles).
Topic: [describe what should stand in the box, e.g. “a beaker of water on a hot plate and boiling chips on the bottom”].
Rules: real sizes (beaker 7 cm wide, plate 16 cm), things do not overlap, apparatus stands on the bottom (y = 0) or on another thing. Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

beakerOnPlate.title: Beaker of water on a hot plate
beakerOnPlate.summary: boiling scene: a beaker of water (20 °C) on a steel hot plate in a box full of air
beakerOnPlate.text:
The beaker holds water at room temperature, with a hot plate under it.
Inspect the particles with the “Inspect” tool — each has its own composition, temperature and mass.

emptyBox.title: Empty box
emptyBox.summary: a box full of air — paint water, put up walls and apparatus
emptyBox.text: The box is full of air. Paint water, draw walls, put up beakers and hot plates.

lab.canvas: {title} — scene; drag bodies, move the background, two fingers zoom
lab.saveFailed: The browser does not allow saving.
lab.jsonNote: This JSON is the scene — paste it in the module editor as “scene”, and the experiment stays on the page.
lab.hintSandbox: Add bodies from the list, drag them, join them with the tools. Start sets time running.
lab.hintExperiment: Tap a body or a tank to see its values. Start sets time running.

toolSays.pin: Tap a body: it gets an axle at that spot (a nail in the wall).
toolSays.rope: Drag from a body to another body or to a point in the air.
toolSays.rod: Drag from a body to another body or to a point: a rigid rod.
toolSays.link: Drag from a body to another body or to a point: a spring.
toolSays.probe: Tap or drag in a liquid: the pressure at that spot.
toolSays.delete: Tap a body to delete it.

ai.prompt:
Prepare a JSON scene for the “Physics lab” module in REcreatio (a school physics experiment in 2D).
Topic: [describe the experiment, e.g. “free fall on the Moon and on Earth”].
Rules: real dimensions and materials; students should do something (run, drag, measure); one phenomenon per scene; labels in English; where it makes sense — values drawn in "vars".
Return ONE JSON object (just the scene). Without comments.

fall.title: Free fall — with air and without
fall.summary: A steel ball, a sheet of paper and a ball fall from the same height — what does the air change?
fall.text:
Three bodies fall from a height of 4 m. Run it and watch the traces: which one falls slowest?
Turn off “Air” in the world settings and repeat (Restart). Without air resistance they all fall the same way — the acceleration is g.
The chart shows the height and speed of the ball: the speed grows evenly (v = g·t).
fall.step1: Let go of all three bodies at once.
fall.step2: Turn off “Air” and restart — compare the traces.

slope.title: Inclined plane and friction
slope.summary: A wooden block and an ice cube on a slope at a random angle: which one slides down?
slope.text:
The angle of the slope is different every time. Predict first: will the wooden block slide? And the ice?
A block slides when tan α is larger than the coefficient of friction (wood on wood: µ ≈ 0.5, i.e. α > 27°; ice: µ ≈ 0.1).
The arrows show the velocity. “New draw” changes the angle.

pendulum.title: Pendulum and conservation of energy
pendulum.summary: A pendulum of random length: the period T = 2π√(L/g) and energy flowing from potential into kinetic.
pendulum.text:
Run it and watch the chart: potential energy (Ep) turns into kinetic energy (Ek), and the sum (E) stays.
Measure the period: how many seconds does one full swing take? Compare with T = 2π√(L/g) — measure the length with the ruler.
Grab the ball and let go from another height.

spring.title: Oscillation on a spring
spring.summary: A weight on a spring of random stiffness: the period T = 2π√(m/k).
spring.text:
The spring has a different stiffness k every time. Pull the weight down and let go.
The height chart is a sine wave. The period depends on the mass and the stiffness: T = 2π√(m/k) — not on how hard you pull.
spring.step1: Pull the weight down and let go.

collisions.title: Collisions on an air table
collisions.summary: Pucks without friction: the momentum before the collision equals the momentum after.
collisions.text:
A table seen from above — without gravity and without friction. The large (steel) puck hits the small one.
Push the pucks (drag and let go). The arrows are velocities. The sum of m·v before and after the collision is the same.
collisions.step1: Run: the steel puck will hit the aluminium one.

cradle.title: Newton’s cradle
cradle.summary: Five steel balls on rods: one strikes, one bounces off.
cradle.text:
Pull back the outer ball and let go. Momentum and energy pass through all the balls — the one on the other side bounces off.
Try with two balls at once.

throw.title: Throw into the basket
throw.summary: Throw the ball (drag and let go) so that it lands in the basket — the path is a parabola.
throw.text:
Grab the ball, swing it with your finger and let go. The trace shows the flight path — a parabola.
The basket stands somewhere else every time.
throw.goal: Basket! The ball’s path is a parabola: uniform motion horizontally and uniformly accelerated motion vertically.

atwood.title: Atwood machine
atwood.summary: Two weights on a rope over a pulley: a = g·(m₁ − m₂)/(m₁ + m₂).
atwood.text:
The heavier weight goes down, the lighter one goes up — with an acceleration smaller than g.
Measure the time of a one-metre drop (ruler) and compare with the formula.

lever.title: Lever — a seesaw
lever.summary: Balance the seesaw: mass × arm on both sides.
lever.text:
A 2 kg and a 4 kg weight lie on the seesaw. Move them so that the seesaw stands level.
Condition for balance: m₁·r₁ = m₂·r₂ (moment of force).

floating.title: Floating bodies
floating.summary: Cork, wood, ice, plastic, aluminium and steel in water — which float, and how deep do they sink?
floating.text:
Run: the blocks fall into the water. Whatever has a lower density than water (1000 kg/m³) floats.
A floating body sinks until it displaces as much water as it weighs itself: submerged part = density of the body / density of water (ice: 92 %).
Arrows: weight (W) and buoyant force (Fb).
floating.step1: Drop the blocks into the water.

archimedes.title: Archimedes’ principle
archimedes.summary: An overflow vessel: the water displaced by the block overflows into a beaker, and the spring scale shows less.
archimedes.text:
The block hangs on a spring (a spring scale). Dip it into the overflow vessel (grab it and lower it).
The water the block displaces flows out into the beaker next to it. The force on the spring drops by exactly the weight of that water — that is the buoyant force.
archimedes.step1: Grab the block and dip it into the water.

pressure.title: Hydrostatic pressure
pressure.summary: A tall tank with three holes: the deeper, the greater the pressure and the farther the jet.
pressure.text:
Open the holes (click the tank, then “Open”). The jet from the lowest hole spurts the farthest.
Pressure grows with depth: p = p₀ + ρ·g·h. Outflow speed: v = √(2·g·h) (Torricelli). Measure the pressure with the probe.
pressure.step3: Open the highest one — compare the jets.

vessels.title: Communicating vessels
vessels.summary: Three vessels of different widths joined by a pipe — the water levels out.
vessels.text:
There is water only in the middle vessel, and the pipes are open. Run it: the levels even out, although the vessels have different widths.
The pressure at the bottom depends only on the height of the water column, not on the shape of the vessel.
vessels.step1: Run it — the water will flow through the pipes.

uTube.title: U-tube with oil and water
uTube.summary: Oil is lighter than water: the oil column is taller than the water on the other side.
uTube.text:
The tube holds water, and the left arm also oil. The levels are not equal!
At the height of the boundary the pressures are equal: ρ_oil·h_oil = ρ_water·h_water.
uTube.step1: Run it and wait until the levels settle.

egg.title: An egg in fresh and salt water
egg.summary: An egg sinks in ordinary water and floats in salt water — the density of the liquid matters.
egg.text:
Two eggs fall into two tanks: one with tap water and one with heavily salted water.
The density of an egg (about 1035 kg/m³) is greater than that of water but smaller than that of brine (1100 kg/m³).

support.denied: Without the „Nearby devices" permission this won't work — you can grant it in the app settings.

console.unchecked: Lamp response not checked — the phone only knows that Android transmitted.
console.asked: requested {ms} ms · a packet every {every} ms

limits.title: What „sent" means — and what the phone cannot do
limits.sent: Sent ≠ the lamp worked. Android only confirms that the BLE advertisement started and was stopped. Whether the lamp heard it, you check yourself (the „Yes/No" buttons in the console).
limits.noAddress: Choosing a device does not address a lamp. A BLE advertisement reaches everything in range. Which lamp switches on is decided by the bytes in the packet (identifier, counter — depending on the manufacturer), not by the name or number here.
limits.noSpoof: The remote's address is not faked. The phone transmits from its own (random) address; a normal app cannot change it. If the lamp checks the sender's address, the packet alone is not enough.
limits.replay: Replay protection. If the remote changes a counter or code on every press, a recorded packet may be rejected.
limits.timing: Timings are approximate. A packet goes out at most every 100 ms — Android does not transmit faster (the pause slider can only make that gap longer); starting and switching between frames take tens of milliseconds. Gaps of a few ms as in the remote are not possible — the console shows how long it really took.
limits.makerOnly: Only manufacturer data (0xFF) is sent unchanged. Android arranges other structures (name, flags, UUID) its own way — such packets are rejected with an explanation, not silently changed.
limits.power: The phone transmits at „high" power, not connectable; 31 bytes is the limit of a legacy advertisement.

node.intro:
Lamps are Bluetooth LE devices controlled by a phone with the REcreatio app (the SMS edition for Android): each device has buttons — signals, i.e. BLE advertisement packets entered by hand or read from the remote. Timers send signals at a set time. A document may contain everything (a backup, a move to another account) or only a part — e.g. just timers prepared by AI.
What the import does:
- It first shows the list of changes with warnings; only „Import” saves. Saving goes the same way as a change by hand: devices and timers are encrypted in the browser with the key of the „Only me” area, and the phone that runs the timers gets the new plan right away.
- An entry with an "id" from the export is changed in place — only the keys the document gives; the rest stays as it was. An entry without "id" (or with an "id" that is not here — e.g. from another account) is created as new, with a new "id" — on every import again, so take a fresh export for further changes.
- It deletes nothing unless an entry with "id" has "remove": true — a device, a signal or a timer; the list of changes shows it.
- An entry with an error (bad packet, no time, action without a device) is skipped with a warning; the rest is saved. Unknown keys also give a warning.
- Whether THIS phone runs the timers is set on the phone (the timer list) — the document does not contain it.
Limits: at most {rows} devices and timers together, {signals} signals in a device, {frames} frames in a signal, {actions} actions in a timer.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

usage.title: How the app uses this data
usage.text:
- Devices and timers live in your „Only me” area, each sealed separately: only you see them, on every device where you sign in; the service only sees that they exist.
- Only a phone with the app in the SMS edition transmits (Bluetooth LE advertisement). In the browser and in the regular app, devices, signals and timers can be set up but not transmitted.
- A timer remembers the device and the signal, not the bytes: a corrected signal also applies in timers as soon as the phone stores the new plan.
- The phone keeps its own timer plan, and the alarm transmits on time — even when the app is closed; „Recent runs” are shown in the timer list on the phone.
- The plan is stored anew after every change made on this phone (also after an import) and when the app starts: an import done in the browser is picked up by the phone the next time the app is opened.
- The button pace ("buttons") is remembered on the account: it applies at once to every press, on every phone; it does not change timers.

frame.title: Frame ("frames[]")
frame.lead: A frame is one packet and how long to transmit it; the frames of a signal go one after another.
frame.text: A packet is a „legacy” BLE advertisement: at most {max} bytes, with one manufacturer data structure — length, FF, manufacturer ID (2 bytes, little endian), data; e.g. "1EFF0000…" is {bytes} with ID 0x0000. The phone does not transmit other structures (flags, names, UUIDs, service data) — the import skips a signal with them. Zeros at the end (padding from listening) are not transmitted.

signal.title: Signal ("signals[]")
signal.lead: A signal is a button: a label and what the phone transmits when it is pressed — one frame or several in order (a sequence). A short press sends the whole signal; holding transmits while the button is held.
signal.text: The import skips a signal with an error (e.g. a bad packet) with a warning — a change to an existing signal is then not applied; the rest of the device is saved.

lamp.title: Device ("lamps[]")
lamp.lead: A device orders the buttons: name, number and room do not select a receiver — a BLE advertisement reaches every lamp in range, and which one switches on is decided by the bytes in the packet.
lamp.text: Signals of an existing device: with "id" they change in place, without "id" they are added, unlisted ones stay. When the document lists ALL signals of the device, its order applies; when only some — new ones are added at the end. Devices appear on the page by number, then by name.

action.title: Timer action ("actions[]")
action.lead: Action: which signal of which device to send.
action.text: "@key" is the "key" of a device or signal in this document; the key the export gives a device and signal (e.g. "@lampa-w-sypialni-nr-1", "@wlacz") also works when the device itself is not in the document. Names are compared ignoring case and Polish characters; a name must point to exactly one device (one signal) — otherwise the action is skipped with a warning. The export writes actions as "@key".

pace.title: Pace ("pace", "buttons")
pace.lead: Pace slows transmission without changing the saved signals. In a timer: { "pauseMs", "limitMs" }; in "buttons" (buttons and test sends, remembered on the account) only "pauseMs" — how long a button transmits is decided by holding it.

timer.title: Timer ("timers[]")
timer.lead: A timer sends signals in order at a given time on chosen days of the week. It is run by a phone with the REcreatio app (SMS edition) on which timers are switched on — even when the app is closed.
timer.text: To change an existing timer, "id" and what changes are enough (e.g. {"id": "…", "enabled": false}). The import skips a timer with a bad time, bad days or no action that points to something (an existing one stays unchanged).

  ## Subheading            (# or ## — subheading, ### — smaller)
  An empty line separates paragraphs; a single line break stays (psalms, hymns).

  [[these words|@key]]     link to an entry with your own words (e.g. [[sermon on bread|@kazanie-chleb]]) — also never a footnote
  ^[footnote text]         your own footnote, without a source
  ![@quote-key]            a quote from the library as a separate block, captioned with where it comes from
  ![@entry-id]             a knowledge-base entry with block content (e.g. a comment) as a separate block — whole, with tables
  [[house|@id-słowa]]      link to a knowledge-base entry (e.g. a word from a dictionary) — the reader sees it if they may read that base

  > text                   indented quote
  - item   ·   1. item
  ---                      separating line
  \sign                    a sign without meaning (e.g. \* instead of italics)
Footnotes number themselves; the first time a source is given in full, then shortened with “op. cit.”, and right after itself — “Ibid.”. A bibliography appears below the text.
{bible}
A source (what came from outside) is cited, your own entries are linked: [@ratzinger2007, s. 183; @kazanie-chleb] gives a footnote to the book and in the text a link “(see Bread of Life)”. What the reader cannot open shows as “[reference unavailable]” (or just the words from [[…|@…]]) — without a title and without a key.
A key is a help while writing: the app remembers a fixed link to the entry (its id), so a later change of the key does not break the text. Instead of a key you can also give the entry's id: [@01a1…-…, s. 3]. A key that does not exist stays in the text as it is (with a warning at import).
describe.head:
# Library as JSON ("{format}", version {version})

What the import does:
The Library is the backbone of citation: it holds ONLY sources — works ("work"), quotes ("quote") and people as authors ("person"); a library entry points only to other library entries (a quote → its work, a work → authors, translators, the book or periodical it is in). Your own texts (sermons, talks, articles) are in the Scriptorium (format "{scriptorium}"), and knowledge — comments, people, places, events — in Knowledge (Cogita), as your own kinds; both cite from here. There are no topics.
- Every entry is { "id", "kind", "key", "data" }. An entry with an id from an export (or with the key of an existing entry of the same kind) is CHANGED — only the fields given in "data"; fields that are missing stay. To clear a field, give null.
- An entry without an id (or with an unknown one) is created new. The import deletes nothing.
- References ("authors", "editors", "translators", "container", "work"; for music "composers", "lyricists", "arrangers", "performers", "piece", "album") can be ids or keys: "@ratzinger2007". Keys from the same document work too — you can describe a whole library without knowing any id.
- Music is also works ("work"), with another type: "piece" (piece), "score" (sheet music), "recording" (recording), "album" (album). The type decides which fields the work has. Sheet music and a recording point to their piece ("piece"), a recording — to its album ("album"). Files (pages of sheet music, tracks of a recording: separate voices and instruments or the whole) are uploaded in the app; JSON describes them without files or carries them from an export. A place in a recording is a time: "1:23", "1:23–1:45".
- A file with other kinds (texts, deliveries, projects, comments, topics) is rejected — with a note where to import it.
- "key" is the citation key: short, without spaces (e.g. "ratzinger2007"); texts refer to it as [@ratzinger2007, s. 23]. Omitted — one will be suggested.
- Numbers may have a unit ("384 s.", "20,5 cm"); a choice field accepts the value ("hard") or its name ("Twarda").
- Quotes from one book (e.g. read by AI from photos) have their own format "{quotes}" — they are imported on that book's page.
- Who sees an entry is decided only by the area of its library: the area's members, and when the area is public — everyone. There are no private fields and no publishing of single entries; what is to stay private goes to the library of a private area.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

{
  "format": "{format}",
  "version": {version},
  "name": "My library",
  "entries": [ { "kind": "person", "key": "ratzinger", "data": { … } }, … ]
}

## Kinds of entries
describe.use:
## How the app uses this data
- In the Library entries stand in the tabs “Sources”, “Music”, “Quotes” and “People”; each has its page, and “Map” draws the connections (quote → work → authors). The code scanner opens a book by "isbn" or by "libraryNumber".
- [@key, place] in a Scriptorium text, in a knowledge-base entry or in a page's “Text” module becomes a footnote (the first time a full description, then a short one); below a Scriptorium text and in print (LaTeX) there is a “Sources” list. ![@quote-key] inserts a quote as a block captioned with where it comes from.
- Texts store the entry's id, not its description: corrected data of a work or person shows at once in every footnote, and changing a key breaks nothing.
- The page module “Quote collection” shows the quotes of this library (or of one work): a “thought of the day” or a collection with search.
- A knowledge base that has this library among its sources points to its entries, and card templates and reviews can use them (e.g. quotes); nothing is copied. In the Scriptorium a text type can have a field that points to a work with a place (e.g. "@bt" and "Łk 1,26-38").
- “Connections” on an entry show what points to it — in libraries, scriptoria and knowledge bases the reader can open.
- The full text of a work comes with a separate import (“Source text”, “Work with text”); then quoted places lead to the paragraph (“show in text”).
- Entries are sealed in the browser with the area key. “AI access” (an area link, MCP server), if it covers this library, gives the assistant a copy of it to read — the assistant searches and reads entries and changes nothing.

quotesDoc.head:
# Quotes of one book as JSON ("{format}", version {version})

What the import does (on the page of the book “{title}”):
- Every quote becomes a “Quote” entry with this book as its source; the citation key is assigned automatically ({key}-1, {key}-2, …).
- Before saving you see the list: every quote can be corrected or unticked.
- A quote already in this book (the same text) is unticked. A quote with an "id" from an export is changed in place.
- The quotes go to this book's library — whoever sees its area sees them. The library holds only sources: quotes have no topics or comments (your own thoughts are a kind in Knowledge).
- Older fields ("topics", "comment", "description", "notes") are only shown while checking — they are not saved.
- Nothing is deleted.
Return ONE JSON object, without comments.

{
  "format": "{format}",
  "version": {version},
  "work": {summary},
  "quotes": [ { … }, … ]
}

## Fields of a quote ("quotes": a list)
quotesDoc.afterFields:
"text" is required. Separate paragraphs in "text" with an empty line.

Example:
quotesDoc.use:
## How the app uses this data
- Quotes stand on the book's page (“Quotes from this book”) in the order of places in the work (pages as numbers, Holy Scripture by the canon) and in the library's “Quotes” tab.
- [@{key}] in a Scriptorium text or in a knowledge-base entry gives a footnote to this book with the quote's place; ![@{key}] inserts the whole quote as a block captioned with where it comes from (also as a plan point).
- The page module “Quote collection” shows the quotes of the library or of this book only: a “thought of the day” (different each day, the same for everyone) or a collection with search.
- When the reader can open the full text of this book and the quote's place is in it, “show in text” stands below the quote.
- A knowledge base that has this library among its sources can make cards and reviews from the quotes; nothing is copied. An entry in Knowledge that points to a quote (e.g. your own comment) shows at the quote under “Connections”.
- Quotes are sealed in the browser with the library's area key. “AI access” (an area link, MCP server), if it covers this library, gives the assistant the quotes to search and read; the assistant changes nothing.

quotesPrompt.marked: The reader marked passages in the book in pencil that they want to keep: underlining, vertical lines or brackets in the margin, exclamation marks, ticks. Transcribe EVERY marked passage as a separate quote. Do not transcribe unmarked text.
quotesPrompt.whole: Each photo shows a passage to keep. Transcribe the whole main text of each photo as a quote (without the running head, the page number and the footnotes at the bottom of the page).
quotesPrompt.intro: The photos show pages of the book: {book}.
quotesPrompt.rules:
Rules:
- Transcribe word for word, as printed: spelling, punctuation, quotation marks. Do not correct, summarise or translate anything.
- Join words hyphenated at the end of a line (“prayer-” + “ful” → “prayerful”). No line breaks inside a paragraph; separate paragraphs with an empty line.
- If a marking starts or ends in the middle of a sentence, transcribe exactly the marked range. Mark an omitted middle with “[…]”.
- A passage that runs onto the next page is ONE quote — "page": "23–24".
- Take the page number from the printed page number of that page. If it is not visible, leave "page" empty and set "uncertain": true.
- Transcribe a reader's handwritten note at the passage in "check" (the passage itself without the note).
- If you are not sure about a word or the edges of a marking: "uncertain": true and briefly in "check" what to check.
- Order of quotes: by page.
